Writing the conclusion
Decision using the critical region (Chapters 1–2 and Section 3.1)

\(t_{\text{cal}}\) = … [falls / does not fall] in the critical region (\(t_{\text{cal}}\) [<, >] …), so we [reject / accept] \(H_0\).

Decision using the p-value (from Section 3.2 onward)

p-value = … [<, \(\ge\)] \(\alpha\) = 0.05, so we [reject / accept] \(H_0\).

Interpretation

That is, … at the 0.05 level of significance.


If we reject \(H_0\), write \(H_1\) as a sentence.
If we accept \(H_0\), write \(H_0\) as a sentence.
For a two-sided test that rejects \(H_0\), also state the direction, using the sample statistic.

Confidence interval

We are 95% confident that … is between … and ….

text:
Distinguish a parameter from a statistic.
Describe the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) and of \(\hat{p}\): its mean, its standard error and its shape.
Calculate the standard error of \(\bar{x}\) and of \(\hat{p}\).
Explain what a 95% confidence interval means.
Write the null and alternative hypotheses for a research question, and tell a one-sided test from a two-sided test.
Find critical values and the critical region from the \(z\) table (Table 4).
Explain Type I and Type II errors in an economic setting.







NoteWhy Does This Matter?



Economists rarely see a whole population. The Ministry of Labour cannot ask every worker in Chiang Mai about their wage, and the Bank of Thailand cannot survey every household about its debt. Instead we take a sample and use it to say something about the population.
Two samples from the same population give different answers. Statistical inference tells us how much a sample result can vary, and so how far we can trust it. This chapter builds the ideas used in every later chapter.

A parameter describes a population. It is a fixed number, but usually unknown. A statistic describes a sample. We can calculate it, but it changes from sample to sample.

The sampling distribution of a statistic is the distribution of its values over all possible samples of the same size \(n\).
Example. Figure 1.1 uses a population of 100,000 households. Monthly household income is skewed to the right: most households earn a moderate amount and a few earn a great deal. The population mean is \(\mu\) = 27,054 baht and the standard deviation is \(\sigma\) = 19,543 baht. The other panels show the means of 5,000 random samples of size 5, 30 and 100.








Figure 1.1: Household income in a population (top left) and the sampling distribution of the sample mean for n = 5, 30 and 100





Three things happen as \(n\) grows:

The sample means are centred on the population mean \(\mu\) (dashed line).
The spread of the sample means gets smaller.
The shape gets closer to a normal curve, even though the population is skewed.

section: 1.2 Standard Error and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
1.2 Standard Error and the Central Limit Theorem
The standard deviation of a sampling distribution is called the standard error (SE). It measures how much a statistic varies from sample to sample.

Sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\)

Mean: \(\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu\)
Standard error: \(\displaystyle \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Shape:

if the population is normal, \(\bar{x}\) is normal for any \(n\);
if not, \(\bar{x}\) is approximately normal when \(n\) is large (\(n \ge 30\)). This is the Central Limit Theorem (CLT).




Sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\)
The sample proportion \(\hat{p} = x/n\), where \(x\) is the number of “successes”.

Mean: \(\mu_{\hat{p}} = p\)
Standard error: \(\displaystyle \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\)
Shape: approximately normal when \(np \ge 5\) and \(n(1-p) \ge 5\).



Example 1.1: daily wage
The daily wage of construction workers in Chiang Mai has mean \(\mu\) = 380 baht and standard deviation \(\sigma\) = 60 baht.

Describe the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) for samples of \(n\) = 36 workers.
Find the standard error for samples of \(n\) = 144 workers.







TipSolution






Since \(n\) = 36 \(\ge 30\), by the CLT \(\bar{x}\) is approximately normal with \[
\mu_{\bar{x}} = 380 \text{ baht}, \qquad
\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{60}{\sqrt{36}} = 10 \text{ baht.}
\]
\[
\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{60}{\sqrt{144}} = 5 \text{ baht.}
\]






Example 1.2: household debt
In a region, 65% of households have outstanding debt. A survey samples \(n\) = 400 households. Describe the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\).






TipSolution





Check the conditions: \(np = 260 \ge 5\) and \(n(1-p) = 140 \ge 5\), so \(\hat{p}\) is approximately normal with mean \(\mu_{\hat{p}} = 0.65\) and \[
\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.65(1-0.65)}{400}} = 0.0238
\]

section: 1.3 The Idea of a Confidence Interval
text:
1.3 The Idea of a Confidence Interval
A single number such as \(\bar{x}\) is a point estimate. It is almost never exactly equal to \(\mu\). A confidence interval (CI) gives a range of plausible values instead: \[
\text{point estimate} \;\pm\; (\text{critical value}) \times \text{SE}
\]
The confidence level (for example 95%) describes the method, not one interval: if we took many samples and built a 95% CI from each, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true parameter.








Figure 1.2: Forty 95% confidence intervals for the mean daily wage, each from a different sample of 36 workers (population mean 380 baht). Red intervals miss the true mean.





In Figure 1.2, 37 of the 40 intervals contain \(\mu\) = 380 and 3 do not. For a single interval we write:

We are 95% confident that the mean daily wage is between … and … baht.







WarningA common mistake



Do not say “there is a 95% probability that \(\mu\) is in this interval”. Once the interval is calculated, \(\mu\) is either in it or not. The 95% refers to how often the method works.


Chapters 2 and 3 give the formula of the CI for each parameter.

1.4 The Logic of Hypothesis Testing
A hypothesis test uses sample data to decide between two statements about a population parameter.

The null hypothesis \(H_0\) is the statement of “no change” or “no difference”. It always contains the equals sign.
The alternative hypothesis \(H_1\) is what the researcher wants to show. It contains \(\ne\), \(<\) or \(>\).

We assume \(H_0\) is true and ask whether the sample result is unusual under that assumption. If it is, we reject \(H_0\).
Example. The Ministry of Labour reports that the mean daily wage of construction workers is 380 baht. A labour union believes the mean is lower. \[
H_0: \mu = 380 \qquad H_1: \mu < 380
\]
The direction in \(H_1\) comes from the research question, never from the data.

Test statistic, critical value and critical region

The test statistic measures how far the sample result is from \(H_0\), in standard errors. For example \(z_{\text{cal}} = (\bar{x} - \mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})\).
The level of significance \(\alpha\) is the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true. We usually use \(\alpha\) = 0.05.
The critical value separates the values of the test statistic that lead to rejecting \(H_0\) from those that do not.
The critical region is the set of values that lead to rejecting \(H_0\).

Decision rule. If \(z_{\text{cal}}\) falls in the critical region, we reject \(H_0\). Otherwise we accept \(H_0\).

A price-monitoring agency checks whether the mean price of a 5-kg bag of rice has changed from 210 baht.
An economist claims that more than 30% of households in Chiang Mai have used a government stimulus measure.
A bank claims that the mean monthly loan payment of its customers is less than 8,000 baht.

\(H_0: p = 0.30 \quad H_1: p > 0.30\) (right-sided)
\(H_0: \mu = 8000 \quad H_1: \mu < 8000\) (left-sided)

text:
1.5 Type I and Type II Errors
The decision is based on a sample, so it can be wrong.









\(H_0\) is true
\(H_0\) is false




Reject \(H_0\)
Type I error (probability \(\alpha\))
Correct decision


Accept \(H_0\)
Correct decision
Type II error (probability \(\beta\))



Example. The government tests whether a stimulus measure increased mean household spending. \(H_0\): the measure had no effect; \(H_1\): the measure increased spending.

Type I error: concluding that the measure worked when it did not. The government may continue an expensive policy that has no effect.
Type II error: concluding that the measure did not work when it did. The government may stop a useful policy.







TipChoosing \(\alpha\)



A smaller \(\alpha\) makes a Type I error less likely but a Type II error more likely, for the same sample size. A larger sample reduces both.

Exercises
1.1 The price of a kilogram of pork at fresh markets has mean 45 baht and standard deviation 4 baht. A random sample of 64 markets is taken.

Describe the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\).
How many markets are needed for the standard error to be 0.25 baht?







TipSolution: Exercise 1.1






Since \(n\) = 64 \(\ge 30\), \(\bar{x}\) is approximately normal with mean 45 baht and \(\sigma_{\bar{x}} = 4/\sqrt{64} = 0.5\) baht.
\(4/\sqrt{n} = 0.25\) gives \(\sqrt{n} = 16\), so \(n\) = 256 markets.

text: 2.1 Mean, \(\sigma\) Known

title: 2  One-Sample Inference
text:
Learning Objectives

Recognize when the \(z\) method for one mean applies.
Construct and interpret a confidence interval for \(\mu\) when \(\sigma\) is known.
Carry out a \(z\) test for \(\mu\) in five steps and write the conclusion.



Concept
Sometimes the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known from a large source, such as a census or many years of administrative records, while the mean may have changed. For example, the spread of daily wages in an industry is fairly stable, but the mean wage changes with prices and minimum-wage policy.
When \(\sigma\) is known, Chapter 1 tells us that \[
z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}
\] follows the standard normal distribution, provided the population is normal or \(n \ge 30\). Both the confidence interval and the test use this result.


Formulas and Conditions
Conditions: \(\sigma\) is known; a random sample; the population is normal or \(n \ge 30\).
\((1-\alpha)100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) \[
\bar{x} \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\] For a 95% CI, \(z_{0.975} = 1.960\); for a 99% CI, \(z_{0.995} = 2.576\).
Test statistic for \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) \[
z_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}
\]







\(H_1\)
Critical region




\(\mu \ne \mu_0\)
\(z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha/2}\) or \(z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha/2}\)


\(\mu < \mu_0\)
\(z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha}\)


\(\mu > \mu_0\)
\(z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha}\)





Example
Example 2.1.1. From many years of Labour Force Survey records, the standard deviation of the daily wage of construction workers in Chiang Mai is \(\sigma\) = 60 baht. A labour union surveys 36 workers and finds a mean daily wage of \(\bar{x}\) = 358.4 baht. The Ministry of Labour reports a mean of 380 baht; the union believes the true mean is lower.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean daily wage.
At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether the mean daily wage is less than 380 baht.







TipSolution





(a) \(n = 36 \ge 30\), so the CLT applies. \[
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{60}{\sqrt{36}} = 10
\] \[
\bar{x} \pm z_{0.975}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
= 358.4 \pm 1.960(10)
= 358.4 \pm 19.6
\] 95% CI: (338.80, 378.00)
We are 95% confident that the mean daily wage of construction workers in Chiang Mai is between 338.80 and 378.00 baht.
(b)
Step 1: Hypotheses. \(H_0: \mu = 380\) \(\quad H_1: \mu < 380\)
Step 2: Level of significance. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3: Test statistic. \[
z_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}
= \frac{358.4 - 380}{10} = -2.160
\]
Step 4: Critical value and critical region. Left-sided test, area 0.05 to the left: \(z_{0.05} = -z_{0.95} = -1.645\). Critical region: \(z_{\text{cal}} < -1.645\).








Figure 2.1: Critical region for Example 2.1.1





Step 5: Decision and interpretation. \(z_{\text{cal}} = -2.160\) falls in the critical region (\(-2.160 < -1.645\)), so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the mean daily wage of construction workers in Chiang Mai is less than 380 baht at the 0.05 level of significance.





Your Turn






NoteYour Turn 2.1.1



The standard deviation of the price of a 5-kg bag of jasmine rice across shops is known to be \(\sigma\) = 12 baht. A price-monitoring agency checks 49 shops and finds a mean price of \(\bar{x}\) = 214.6 baht.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean price.
At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether the mean price is different from 210 baht.









TipSolution: Your Turn 2.1.1





(a) \(\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 12/\sqrt{49} = 1.7143\); \(214.6 \pm 1.960(1.7143) = 214.6 \pm 3.36\). 95% CI: (211.24, 217.96). We are 95% confident that the mean price of a 5-kg bag of jasmine rice is between 211.24 and 217.96 baht.
(b)
Step 1. \(H_0: \mu = 210 \quad H_1: \mu \ne 210\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3. \(z_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{214.6 - 210}{1.7143} = 2.683\)
Step 4. \(z_{0.025} = -1.960\), \(z_{0.975} = 1.960\). Critical region: \(z_{\text{cal}} < -1.960\) or \(z_{\text{cal}} > 1.960\).
Step 5. \(z_{\text{cal}} = 2.683\) falls in the critical region (\(2.683 > 1.960\)), so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the mean price of a 5-kg bag of jasmine rice is different from 210 baht at the 0.05 level of significance; since \(\bar{x}\) = 214.6, the mean price is higher than 210 baht.





Formula Summary








Formula




Conditions
\(\sigma\) known; population normal or \(n \ge 30\)


\((1-\alpha)100\%\) CI for \(\mu\)
\(\bar{x} \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\sigma/\sqrt{n}\)


Test statistic
\(z_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\)


Critical region
\(\ne\): \(z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha/2}\) or \(z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha/2}\); \(<\): \(z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha}\); \(>\): \(z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha}\)





Exercises
2.1.1 Utility records show that the standard deviation of the monthly electricity bill of households in a city is 320 baht. A sample of 64 households has a mean bill of 1,240 baht. Construct a 99% confidence interval for the mean monthly bill.






TipSolution: Exercise 2.1.1





\(\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 320/\sqrt{64} = 40\); \(z_{0.995} = 2.576\). \(1240 \pm 2.576(40) = 1240 \pm 103.04\). 99% CI: (1,136.96, 1,343.04). We are 99% confident that the mean monthly electricity bill is between 1,136.96 and 1,343.04 baht.



2.1.2 A company claims that the mean monthly sales per salesperson are more than 150 thousand baht. The standard deviation is known to be 24 thousand baht. A sample of 40 salespeople has a mean of 156.2 thousand baht. Test the claim at \(\alpha\) = 0.01.






TipSolution: Exercise 2.1.2





Step 1. \(H_0: \mu = 150 \quad H_1: \mu > 150\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.01
Step 3. \(\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 24/\sqrt{40} = 3.7947\); \(z_{\text{cal}} = (156.2 - 150)/3.7947 = 1.634\)
Step 4. \(z_{0.99} = 2.326\). Critical region: \(z_{\text{cal}} > 2.326\).
Step 5. \(z_{\text{cal}} = 1.634\) does not fall in the critical region (\(1.634 < 2.326\)), so we accept \(H_0\). That is, the mean monthly sales per salesperson are equal to 150 thousand baht at the 0.01 level of significance.



2.1.3 The standard deviation of savings deposits at a bank is known to be 12,000 baht. A sample of 100 accounts has a mean balance of 52,100 baht.

At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether the mean balance is different from 50,000 baht.
Construct a 95% CI for the mean balance. Does it agree with (a)?







TipSolution: Exercise 2.1.3





(a) \(H_0: \mu = 5\times 10^{4} \quad H_1: \mu \ne 5\times 10^{4}\); \(\alpha\) = 0.05. \(\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 1200\); \(z_{\text{cal}} = (5.21\times 10^{4} - 5\times 10^{4})/1200 = 1.750\). Critical region: \(z_{\text{cal}} < -1.960\) or \(z_{\text{cal}} > 1.960\). \(z_{\text{cal}}\) does not fall in the critical region (\(-1.960 < 1.750 < 1.960\)), so we accept \(H_0\). That is, the mean balance is equal to 50,000 baht at the 0.05 level of significance.
(b) \(5.21\times 10^{4} \pm 1.960(1200)\): 95% CI (49,748.00, 54,452.00). The interval contains 50,000, which agrees with accepting \(H_0\) in (a).

title: 2  One-Sample Inference
text:
2.2 Mean, \(\sigma\) Unknown

Learning Objectives

Use the \(t\) distribution when \(\sigma\) is unknown and read the \(t\) table (Table 5).
Construct and interpret a confidence interval for \(\mu\) using \(s\).
Carry out a \(t\) test for \(\mu\) in five steps.
Use a confidence interval to reach the decision of a two-sided test.



Concept
In practice \(\sigma\) is almost never known. We replace it by the sample standard deviation \(s\). Because \(s\) itself varies from sample to sample, the statistic \[
t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s/\sqrt{n}}
\] is more spread out than \(z\). It follows a \(t\) distribution with \(\text{df} = n - 1\) degrees of freedom, provided the population is normal. For moderate or large \(n\) the method still works well when the population is not exactly normal.








Figure 2.2: The t distribution has heavier tails than z; with more df it gets closer to z







Formulas and Conditions
Conditions: \(\sigma\) unknown; a random sample; the population is approximately normal (less important when \(n\) is large).
\((1-\alpha)100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) \[
\bar{x} \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
Test statistic for \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\), with \(\text{df} = n-1\) \[
t_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}
\]







\(H_1\)
Critical region




\(\mu \ne \mu_0\)
\(t_{\text{cal}} < t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\) or \(t_{\text{cal}} > t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\)


\(\mu < \mu_0\)
\(t_{\text{cal}} < t_{\alpha,\,n-1}\)


\(\mu > \mu_0\)
\(t_{\text{cal}} > t_{1-\alpha,\,n-1}\)





Reading the \(t\) Table
Table 5 gives \(t\) values with a stated area to the left (columns) for each df (rows). Like \(z\), the \(t\) curve is symmetric, so the table lists only the right half: \(t_{0.05,\,\text{df}} = -t_{0.95,\,\text{df}}\).






WarningNot every df is in the table



After df = 30 the table jumps to 40, 50, 60, 80, 100, 200, 500 and \(\infty\). All examples in this book use df that appear in the table.


Example 2.2.1. Find (a) \(t_{0.975,\,24}\), (b) \(t_{0.05,\,15}\), (c) \(t_{0.995,\,40}\).






TipSolution






Row df = 24, column 0.975: \(t_{0.975,\,24} = 2.064\).
Area 0.05 is in the left tail. By symmetry, \(t_{0.05,\,15} = -t_{0.95,\,15} = -1.753\).
Row df = 40, column 0.995: \(t_{0.995,\,40} = 2.704\).










NoteYour Turn 2.2.1



Find (a) \(t_{0.975,\,15}\), (b) \(t_{0.01,\,20}\), (c) \(t_{0.95,\,60}\).





















TipSolution: Your Turn 2.2.1






\(t_{0.975,\,15} = 2.131\)
\(t_{0.01,\,20} = -t_{0.99,\,20} = -2.528\)
\(t_{0.95,\,60} = 1.671\)






Example
Example 2.2.2. A food-delivery platform claims that its riders in Chiang Mai earn more than 600 baht per day on average. A researcher records the daily earnings (baht) of 25 randomly selected riders:

The sample gives \(\bar{x}\) = 644.96 and \(s\) = 96.6499 baht.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean daily earnings.
At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test the platform’s claim.







TipSolution





(a) \(\text{df} = 25 - 1 = 24\) and \(t_{0.975,\,24} = 2.064\). \[
\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{96.6499}{\sqrt{25}} = 19.33
\] \[
\bar{x} \pm t_{0.975,\,24}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
= 644.96 \pm 2.064(19.33)
= 644.96 \pm 39.8971
\] 95% CI: (605.06, 684.86)
We are 95% confident that the mean daily earnings of riders in Chiang Mai are between 605.06 and 684.86 baht.
(b)
Step 1: Hypotheses. \(H_0: \mu = 600\) \(\quad H_1: \mu > 600\)
Step 2: Level of significance. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3: Test statistic. \[
t_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}
= \frac{644.96 - 600}{19.33} = 2.326
\]
Step 4: Critical value and critical region. Right-sided test with df = 24: \(t_{0.95,\,24} = 1.711\). Critical region: \(t_{\text{cal}} > 1.711\).








Figure 2.3: Critical region for Example 2.2.2





Step 5: Decision and interpretation. \(t_{\text{cal}} = 2.326\) falls in the critical region (\(2.326 > 1.711\)), so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the mean daily earnings of riders in Chiang Mai are more than 600 baht at the 0.05 level of significance.





Confidence Intervals and Two-Sided Tests
A \((1-\alpha)100\%\) CI and a two-sided test at level \(\alpha\) always agree:

if \(\mu_0\) is outside the CI, a two-sided test rejects \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\);
if \(\mu_0\) is inside the CI, the test accepts \(H_0\).

For the riders, the 95% CI (605.06, 684.86) does not contain 600, so a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = 600\) at \(\alpha\) = 0.05 would reject \(H_0\). It does contain 620, so the same test of \(H_0: \mu = 620\) would accept \(H_0\).






WarningOnly for two-sided tests



This shortcut matches a two-sided test with the same \(\alpha\) as the confidence level (\(\alpha\) = 0.05 with a 95% CI). For a one-sided test, carry out the five steps.




Your Turn






NoteYour Turn 2.2.2



A property agent records the monthly rent of 16 one-bedroom condominium units near Nimmanhaemin Road, Chiang Mai. The sample mean is 9,420 baht and the standard deviation is 784 baht. Assume rents are normally distributed.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean rent.
At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether the mean rent is different from 9,000 baht.
Does the CI in (a) agree with your decision in (b)?









TipSolution: Your Turn 2.2.2





(a) df = 15, \(t_{0.975,\,15} = 2.131\); \(s/\sqrt{n} = 784/\sqrt{16} = 196\); \(9420 \pm 2.131(196) = 9420 \pm 417.676\). 95% CI: (9,002.32, 9,837.68). We are 95% confident that the mean monthly rent is between 9,002.32 and 9,837.68 baht.
(b)
Step 1. \(H_0: \mu = 9000 \quad H_1: \mu \ne 9000\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3. \(t_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{9420 - 9000}{196} = 2.143\)
Step 4. df = 15: \(t_{0.025,\,15} = -2.131\), \(t_{0.975,\,15} = 2.131\). Critical region: \(t_{\text{cal}} < -2.131\) or \(t_{\text{cal}} > 2.131\).
Step 5. \(t_{\text{cal}} = 2.143\) falls in the critical region (\(2.143 > 2.131\)), so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the mean monthly rent is different from 9,000 baht at the 0.05 level of significance; since \(\bar{x}\) = 9,420, the mean rent is higher than 9,000 baht.
(c) Yes. The 95% CI does not contain 9,000, so the two-sided test at \(\alpha\) = 0.05 rejects \(H_0\).





Formula Summary








Formula




Conditions
\(\sigma\) unknown; population approximately normal


\((1-\alpha)100\%\) CI for \(\mu\)
\(\bar{x} \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,s/\sqrt{n}\)


Test statistic
\(t_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}\), df \(= n-1\)


Critical region
\(\ne\): \(t_{\text{cal}} < t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\) or \(t_{\text{cal}} > t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\); \(<\): \(t_{\text{cal}} < t_{\alpha,\,n-1}\); \(>\): \(t_{\text{cal}} > t_{1-\alpha,\,n-1}\)


CI and test
two-sided test at \(\alpha\) rejects \(H_0\) \(\iff\) \(\mu_0\) is outside the \((1-\alpha)100\%\) CI





Exercises
2.2.1 A survey of 20 households in a district finds a mean household debt of 184,500 baht with a standard deviation of 41,200 baht. At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether the mean household debt is more than 170,000 baht.






TipSolution: Exercise 2.2.1





Step 1. \(H_0: \mu = 1.7\times 10^{5} \quad H_1: \mu > 1.7\times 10^{5}\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3. \(s/\sqrt{n} = 4.12\times 10^{4}/\sqrt{20} = 9212.6001\); \(t_{\text{cal}} = (1.845\times 10^{5} - 1.7\times 10^{5})/9212.6001 = 1.574\)
Step 4. df = 19: \(t_{0.95,\,19} = 1.729\). Critical region: \(t_{\text{cal}} > 1.729\).
Step 5. \(t_{\text{cal}} = 1.574\) does not fall in the critical region (\(1.574 < 1.729\)), so we accept \(H_0\). That is, the mean household debt in the district is equal to 170,000 baht at the 0.05 level of significance.



2.2.2 A sample of 30 gig workers reports a mean of 47.3 working hours per week with a standard deviation of 8.4 hours. Construct a 99% confidence interval for the mean weekly working hours.






TipSolution: Exercise 2.2.2





df = 29, \(t_{0.995,\,29} = 2.756\); \(s/\sqrt{n} = 8.4/\sqrt{30} = 1.5336\); \(47.3 \pm 2.756(1.5336) = 47.3 \pm 4.2266\). 99% CI: (43.07, 51.53). We are 99% confident that the mean weekly working hours of gig workers are between 43.07 and 51.53 hours.



2.2.3 A 95% confidence interval for the mean monthly interest rate charged by informal lenders is (12.4%, 15.8%). Without further calculation, what is the decision of a two-sided test at \(\alpha\) = 0.05 for (a) \(H_0: \mu = 16\), (b) \(H_0: \mu = 15\)?






TipSolution: Exercise 2.2.3






16 is outside the CI, so we reject \(H_0\).
15 is inside the CI, so we accept \(H_0\).




2.2.4 Find (a) \(t_{0.90,\,12}\), (b) \(t_{0.025,\,8}\), (c) \(t_{0.99,\,100}\).






TipSolution: Exercise 2.2.4






1.356 (b) \(-t_{0.975,\,8} = -2.306\) (c) 2.364

title: 2  One-Sample Inference
text:
2.3 Proportion

Learning Objectives

Check the conditions for the normal approximation to \(\hat{p}\).
Construct and interpret a confidence interval for a population proportion \(p\).
Carry out a \(z\) test for \(p\) in five steps.
Explain why the CI uses \(\hat{p}\) in the standard error but the test uses \(p_0\).



Concept
Many economic questions are about proportions: the share of households in debt, the labour force participation rate, the share of firms that raised prices, or the share of people who used a stimulus measure. Each person or firm either has the characteristic (“success”) or not.
With \(x\) successes in a sample of \(n\), the sample proportion is \(\hat{p} = x/n\). From Chapter 1, \(\hat{p}\) is approximately normal with mean \(p\) and standard error \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\) when the sample is large enough.






ImportantWhich proportion goes in the standard error?



The standard error contains the unknown \(p\), so we must put in a value:

Confidence interval: we do not assume any value of \(p\), so we use our best estimate \(\hat{p}\).
Hypothesis test: we assume \(H_0\) is true, so we use \(p_0\).





Formulas and Conditions
\((1-\alpha)100\%\) confidence interval for \(p\) \[
\hat{p} \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}
\qquad \text{condition: } n\hat{p} \ge 5 \text{ and } n(1-\hat{p}) \ge 5
\]
Test statistic for \(H_0: p = p_0\) \[
z_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}
\qquad \text{condition: } np_0 \ge 5 \text{ and } n(1-p_0) \ge 5
\]
The critical regions are the same as for the \(z\) test of a mean.


Example
Example 2.3.1. The government ran a co-payment scheme in which it paid part of the price of goods bought at small shops. An economist claims that more than 30% of households in Chiang Mai used the scheme. In a random sample of 400 households, 148 used it.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of households that used the scheme.
At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test the economist’s claim.







TipSolution





\(\hat{p} = 148/400 = 0.37\)
(a) Check: \(n\hat{p} = 148 \ge 5\) and \(n(1-\hat{p}) = 252 \ge 5\). \[
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.37(0.63)}{400}} = 0.0241
\] \[
0.37 \pm 1.960(0.0241) = 0.37 \pm 0.0472
\] 95% CI: (0.3228, 0.4172)
We are 95% confident that the proportion of households in Chiang Mai that used the scheme is between 0.3228 and 0.4172.
(b)
Step 1: Hypotheses. \(H_0: p = 0.30\) \(\quad H_1: p > 0.30\)
Step 2: Level of significance. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3: Test statistic. Check: \(np_0 = 120 \ge 5\) and \(n(1-p_0) = 280 \ge 5\). \[
\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.30(0.70)}{400}} = 0.0229
\] \[
z_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}} = \frac{0.37 - 0.30}{0.0229} = 3.057
\]
Step 4: Critical value and critical region. \(z_{0.95} = 1.645\). Critical region: \(z_{\text{cal}} > 1.645\).
Step 5: Decision and interpretation. \(z_{\text{cal}} = 3.057\) falls in the critical region (\(3.057 > 1.645\)), so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the proportion of households in Chiang Mai that used the scheme is more than 0.30 at the 0.05 level of significance.





Your Turn






NoteYour Turn 2.3.1



A university reports that 70% of its economics graduates find a job within six months. A survey of 250 recent graduates finds that 160 found a job within six months.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of graduates who find a job within six months.
At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether the proportion is different from 0.70.









TipSolution: Your Turn 2.3.1





\(\hat{p} = 160/250 = 0.64\)
(a) \(\sqrt{0.64(0.36)/250} = 0.0304\); \(0.64 \pm 1.960(0.0304) = 0.64 \pm 0.0596\). 95% CI: (0.5804, 0.6996). We are 95% confident that the proportion of graduates who find a job within six months is between 0.5804 and 0.6996.
(b)
Step 1. \(H_0: p = 0.70 \quad H_1: p \ne 0.70\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3. \(\sqrt{0.70(0.30)/250} = 0.029\); \(z_{\text{cal}} = (0.64 - 0.70)/0.029 = -2.069\)
Step 4. Critical region: \(z_{\text{cal}} < -1.960\) or \(z_{\text{cal}} > 1.960\).
Step 5. \(z_{\text{cal}} = -2.069\) falls in the critical region (\(-2.069 < -1.960\)), so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the proportion of graduates who find a job within six months is different from 0.70 at the 0.05 level of significance; since \(\hat{p}\) = 0.64, the proportion is lower than 0.70.





Formula Summary









Confidence interval
Hypothesis test




Standard error
\(\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}\)
\(\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}\)


Condition
\(n\hat{p} \ge 5\), \(n(1-\hat{p}) \ge 5\)
\(np_0 \ge 5\), \(n(1-p_0) \ge 5\)


Formula
\(\hat{p} \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}\)
\(z_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{\hat{p}-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}\)





Exercises
2.3.1 In a survey of 500 small businesses, 95 had borrowed from an informal lender in the past year. Construct a 99% confidence interval for the proportion of small businesses that borrowed from an informal lender.






TipSolution: Exercise 2.3.1





\(\hat{p} = 0.19\); \(\sqrt{0.19(0.81)/500} = 0.0175\); \(z_{0.995} = 2.576\); \(0.19 \pm 2.576(0.0175) = 0.19 \pm 0.0451\). 99% CI: (0.1449, 0.2351). We are 99% confident that the proportion of small businesses that borrowed from an informal lender is between 0.1449 and 0.2351.



2.3.2 A bank believes that less than 25% of its credit-card holders pay only the minimum amount each month. In a sample of 300 card holders, 66 paid only the minimum. Test the bank’s belief at \(\alpha\) = 0.05.






TipSolution: Exercise 2.3.2





Step 1. \(H_0: p = 0.25 \quad H_1: p < 0.25\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3. \(\hat{p} = 0.22\); \(\sqrt{0.25(0.75)/300} = 0.025\); \(z_{\text{cal}} = (0.22 - 0.25)/0.025 = -1.200\)
Step 4. \(z_{0.05} = -1.645\). Critical region: \(z_{\text{cal}} < -1.645\).
Step 5. \(z_{\text{cal}} = -1.200\) does not fall in the critical region (\(-1.200 > -1.645\)), so we accept \(H_0\). That is, the proportion of card holders who pay only the minimum is equal to 0.25 at the 0.05 level of significance.



2.3.3 A researcher wants to test \(H_0: p = 0.05\) for the unemployment rate in a district using a sample of 60 people. Is the \(z\) test appropriate? Explain.






TipSolution: Exercise 2.3.3





No. \(np_0 = 60(0.05) = 3 < 5\), so the normal approximation is not reliable. A larger sample (at least 100 people) is needed.

title: 2  One-Sample Inference
text:
2.4 Variance

Learning Objectives

Explain why the variance matters in economics (risk, volatility, price stability).
Read the chi-square table (Table 6).
Construct and interpret a confidence interval for \(\sigma^2\) and \(\sigma\).
Carry out a chi-square test for \(\sigma^2\) in five steps.



Concept
The mean tells us the typical value; the variance tells us how much values vary. In finance the standard deviation of returns is the most common measure of risk (volatility). A central bank cares about the stability of prices, and a firm cares about the stability of its sales.
To make inferences about \(\sigma^2\) we use the sample variance \(s^2\). If the population is normal, \[
\chi^2 = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma^2}
\] follows a chi-square distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom. The chi-square distribution takes only positive values and is skewed to the right.








Figure 2.4: Chi-square distributions are skewed to the right; the skew decreases as df increases











WarningThe population must be normal



The chi-square methods for a variance are sensitive to non-normality, even for large samples. Use them only when the data are approximately normal.




Reading the Chi-Square Table
Table 6 gives \(\chi^2\) values with a stated area to the left, for df = 1 to 100. The curve is not symmetric, so for a two-sided test or a CI we read two different values from the table; we cannot use a minus sign.
Example 2.4.1. For df = 23, find \(\chi^2_{0.025,\,23}\), \(\chi^2_{0.975,\,23}\) and \(\chi^2_{0.95,\,23}\).






TipSolution





Row df = 23: \(\chi^2_{0.025,\,23} = 11.7\), \(\chi^2_{0.975,\,23} = 38.1\) and \(\chi^2_{0.95,\,23} = 35.2\).








Figure 2.5: Areas 0.025 in each tail of the chi-square distribution with df = 23














NoteYour Turn 2.4.1



Find (a) \(\chi^2_{0.05,\,19}\), (b) \(\chi^2_{0.995,\,10}\), (c) \(\chi^2_{0.025,\,30}\).





















TipSolution: Your Turn 2.4.1






\(\chi^2_{0.05,\,19} = 10.1\)
\(\chi^2_{0.995,\,10} = 25.2\)
\(\chi^2_{0.025,\,30} = 16.8\)






Formulas and Conditions
Condition: a random sample from a normal population.
\((1-\alpha)100\%\) confidence interval for \(\sigma^2\) \[
\left(\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}},\;
      \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}}\right)
\] Take the square root of both limits to get a CI for \(\sigma\). The larger chi-square value gives the lower limit. The interval is not symmetric about \(s^2\).
Test statistic for \(H_0: \sigma^2 = \sigma_0^2\), with df \(= n-1\) \[
\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}
\]







\(H_1\)
Critical region




\(\sigma^2 \ne \sigma_0^2\)
\(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} < \chi^2_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\) or \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} > \chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\)


\(\sigma^2 < \sigma_0^2\)
\(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} < \chi^2_{\alpha,\,n-1}\)


\(\sigma^2 > \sigma_0^2\)
\(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} > \chi^2_{1-\alpha,\,n-1}\)



A claim about \(\sigma\) is tested as the same claim about \(\sigma^2\): for example \(\sigma > 2\) is \(\sigma^2 > 4\).


Example
Example 2.4.2. A fund manager states that the standard deviation of the fund’s monthly return is 2%. An investor suspects the fund is riskier. Over the last 24 months the standard deviation of the monthly return was \(s\) = 2.6%. Assume monthly returns are normally distributed.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for the variance and the standard deviation of the monthly return.
At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether the standard deviation is more than 2%.







TipSolution





\(s^2 = 2.6^2 = 6.76\), df = 23, \((n-1)s^2 = 23(6.76) = 155.48\).
(a) \(\chi^2_{0.025,\,23} = 11.7\) and \(\chi^2_{0.975,\,23} = 38.1\). \[
\left(\frac{155.48}{38.1},\; \frac{155.48}{11.7}\right)
= (4.0808,\; 13.2889)
\] For \(\sigma\): \((\sqrt{4.0808},\ \sqrt{13.2889}) = (2.0201,\ 3.6454)\)
We are 95% confident that the standard deviation of the fund’s monthly return is between 2.0201% and 3.6454%. Note that \(s\) = 2.6 is not in the middle of the interval.
(b)
Step 1: Hypotheses. \(H_0: \sigma^2 = 4\) \(\quad H_1: \sigma^2 > 4\) (that is, \(\sigma > 2\))
Step 2: Level of significance. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3: Test statistic. \[
\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2} = \frac{155.48}{4} = 38.870
\]
Step 4: Critical value and critical region. df = 23: \(\chi^2_{0.95,\,23} = 35.2\). Critical region: \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} > 35.2\).
Step 5: Decision and interpretation. \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = 38.870\) falls in the critical region (\(38.870 > 35.2\)), so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the standard deviation of the fund’s monthly return is more than 2% at the 0.05 level of significance.





Your Turn






NoteYour Turn 2.4.2



A price-stabilization policy aims to keep the standard deviation of the weekly retail price of pork at 3 baht per kg. Over 20 weeks the standard deviation was \(s\) = 4.5 baht. Assume prices are normally distributed.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\sigma\).
At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether the standard deviation is different from 3 baht.









TipSolution: Your Turn 2.4.2





\(s^2 = 20.25\), df = 19, \((n-1)s^2 = 384.75\); \(\chi^2_{0.025,\,19} = 8.91\), \(\chi^2_{0.975,\,19} = 32.9\).
(a) CI for \(\sigma^2\): \((384.75/32.9,\ 384.75/8.91) = (11.6945,\ 43.1818)\). CI for \(\sigma\): (3.4197, 6.5713). We are 95% confident that the standard deviation of the weekly pork price is between 3.4197 and 6.5713 baht.
(b)
Step 1. \(H_0: \sigma^2 = 9 \quad H_1: \sigma^2 \ne 9\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3. \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = 384.75/9 = 42.750\)
Step 4. Critical region: \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} < 8.91\) or \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} > 32.9\).
Step 5. \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = 42.750\) falls in the critical region (\(42.750 > 32.9\)), so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the standard deviation of the weekly pork price is different from 3 baht at the 0.05 level of significance; since \(s\) = 4.5, it is higher than 3 baht, so the policy target was not met.

2.4.1 Before a new ordering system, the standard deviation of a shop’s daily sales was 10 units. After the system was introduced, 16 days of sales had a standard deviation of 7.2 units. At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether the standard deviation is now less than 10 units. Assume normality.






TipSolution: Exercise 2.4.1





Step 1. \(H_0: \sigma^2 = 100 \quad H_1: \sigma^2 < 100\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3. \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = 15(51.84)/100 = 7.776\)
Step 4. \(\chi^2_{0.05,\,15} = 7.26\). Critical region: \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} < 7.26\).
Step 5. \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = 7.776\) does not fall in the critical region (\(7.776 > 7.26\)), so we accept \(H_0\). That is, the standard deviation of daily sales is equal to 10 units at the 0.05 level of significance.



2.4.2 The daily change in an exchange rate over 25 trading days has a standard deviation of 0.35 baht. Assuming normality, construct a 90% confidence interval for the standard deviation of the daily change.






TipSolution: Exercise 2.4.2





\((n-1)s^2 = 24(0.1225) = 2.94\); \(\chi^2_{0.05,\,24} = 13.8\), \(\chi^2_{0.95,\,24} = 36.4\). CI for \(\sigma^2\): (0.0808, 0.2130); CI for \(\sigma\): (0.2843, 0.4615). We are 90% confident that the standard deviation of the daily change is between 0.2843 and 0.4615 baht.



2.4.3 Explain why the confidence interval for \(\sigma^2\) is not of the form “estimate \(\pm\) margin of error”.






TipSolution: Exercise 2.4.3





The chi-square distribution is skewed to the right, so the two critical values are not the same distance from the centre. Dividing \((n-1)s^2\) by them gives limits that are not equally far from \(s^2\).

title: 3  Two-Sample Inference
text:
Learning Objectives

Construct and interpret a confidence interval for the difference \(p_1 - p_2\).
Carry out a \(z\) test for \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) using the pooled proportion.
Explain why the test pools the two samples but the CI does not.



Concept
We often compare two groups: urban and rural households, men and women in the labour force, customers of two brands. The parameter of interest is the difference \(p_1 - p_2\), estimated by \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\). For two independent random samples that are large enough, \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) is approximately normal with standard error \[
\sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}.
\]
The same idea as in Section 2.3 decides which values go into the standard error:

Confidence interval: use \(\hat{p}_1\) and \(\hat{p}_2\) separately.
Hypothesis test: \(H_0\) says \(p_1 = p_2\), so both groups share one proportion. Our best estimate of it combines the two samples, the pooled proportion \[
\bar{p} = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{n_1 + n_2}.
\]



Formulas and Conditions
Conditions: two independent random samples; \(n\hat{p} \ge 5\) and \(n(1-\hat{p}) \ge 5\) in each sample.
\((1-\alpha)100\%\) confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) \[
(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}
\]
Test statistic for \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) \[
z_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2}
{\sqrt{\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}\right)}}
\]







\(H_1\)
Critical region




\(p_1 \ne p_2\)
\(z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha/2}\) or \(z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha/2}\)


\(p_1 < p_2\)
\(z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha}\)


\(p_1 > p_2\)
\(z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha}\)





Example
Example 3.1.1. A survey asks households whether they have any outstanding debt. In urban areas, 171 of 300 households have debt; in rural areas, 165 of 250 households have debt.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for the difference between the urban and rural proportions.
At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether the proportion of households with debt is different in urban and rural areas.







TipSolution





Let group 1 = urban and group 2 = rural. \(\hat{p}_1 = 171/300 = 0.57\), \(\hat{p}_2 = 165/250 = 0.66\), \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = -0.09\).
(a) \[
\sqrt{\frac{0.57(0.43)}{300} + \frac{0.66(0.34)}{250}} = 0.0414
\] \[
-0.09 \pm 1.960(0.0414) = -0.09 \pm 0.0811
\] 95% CI: (-0.1711, -0.0089)
We are 95% confident that the difference between the urban and rural proportions of households with debt is between -0.1711 and -0.0089. Both limits are negative, so the urban proportion is lower.
(b)
Step 1: Hypotheses. \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) \(\quad H_1: p_1 \ne p_2\)
Step 2: Level of significance. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3: Test statistic. \[
\bar{p} = \frac{171 + 165}{300 + 250} = 0.6109
\] \[
z_{\text{cal}} = \frac{-0.09}
{\sqrt{0.6109(0.3891)\left(\frac{1}{300} + \frac{1}{250}\right)}}
= \frac{-0.09}{0.0418} = -2.153
\]
Step 4: Critical value and critical region. Critical region: \(z_{\text{cal}} < -1.960\) or \(z_{\text{cal}} > 1.960\).
Step 5: Decision and interpretation. \(z_{\text{cal}} = -2.153\) falls in the critical region (\(-2.153 < -1.960\)), so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the proportion of households with debt is different in urban and rural areas at the 0.05 level of significance; since \(\hat{p}_1 < \hat{p}_2\), the proportion is lower in urban areas.





Your Turn






NoteYour Turn 3.1.1



Two brands of instant noodles raised their prices by the same amount. Of 200 regular customers of Brand A, 58 switched to another brand; of 180 regular customers of Brand B, 36 switched.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for \(p_A - p_B\).
At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether the proportion of customers who switched is higher for Brand A.









TipSolution: Your Turn 3.1.1





\(\hat{p}_A = 0.29\), \(\hat{p}_B = 0.2\), \(\hat{p}_A - \hat{p}_B = 0.09\).
(a) SE \(= 0.0438\); \(0.09 \pm 1.960(0.0438) = 0.09 \pm 0.0858\). 95% CI: (0.0042, 0.1758). We are 95% confident that the difference between the proportions of Brand A and Brand B customers who switched is between 0.0042 and 0.1758.
(b)
Step 1. \(H_0: p_A = p_B \quad H_1: p_A > p_B\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3. \(\bar{p} = (58 + 36)/(200 + 180) = 0.2474\); \(z_{\text{cal}} = 0.09/0.0443 = 2.032\)
Step 4. \(z_{0.95} = 1.645\). Critical region: \(z_{\text{cal}} > 1.645\).
Step 5. \(z_{\text{cal}} = 2.032\) falls in the critical region (\(2.032 > 1.645\)), so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the proportion of customers who switched is higher for Brand A than for Brand B at the 0.05 level of significance.

Exercises
3.1.1 In a labour force survey, 45 of 150 women and 62 of 160 men aged 15–24 were not in employment, education or training. Construct a 90% confidence interval for \(p_{\text{women}} - p_{\text{men}}\).






TipSolution: Exercise 3.1.1





\(\hat{p}_1 = 0.3\), \(\hat{p}_2 = 0.3875\), difference \(= -0.0875\), SE \(= 0.0537\), \(z_{0.95} = 1.645\). \(-0.0875 \pm 0.0883\): 90% CI (-0.1758, 0.0008). We are 90% confident that the difference between the proportions of women and men not in employment, education or training is between -0.1758 and 0.0008. The interval contains 0.



3.1.2 A shop tests two price displays. With display 1, 84 of 240 visitors bought the product; with display 2, 96 of 240 bought it. At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether display 1 has a lower purchase rate.






TipSolution: Exercise 3.1.2





Step 1. \(H_0: p_1 = p_2 \quad H_1: p_1 < p_2\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3. \(\hat{p}_1 = 0.35\), \(\hat{p}_2 = 0.4\), \(\bar{p} = 0.375\); \(z_{\text{cal}} = -0.05/0.0442 = -1.131\)
Step 4. \(z_{0.05} = -1.645\). Critical region: \(z_{\text{cal}} < -1.645\).
Step 5. \(z_{\text{cal}} = -1.131\) does not fall in the critical region (\(-1.131 > -1.645\)), so we accept \(H_0\). That is, the purchase rates with the two displays are equal at the 0.05 level of significance.

3.2 P-values

Learning Objectives

Explain what a p-value is.
Find the p-value of a \(z\) test from Table 4 for a left-sided, right-sided or two-sided test.
Make the decision of a test with the p-value, and check that it agrees with the critical region.



Concept
So far we have decided by checking whether the test statistic falls in the critical region. A second way, used by all statistical software, is the p-value.






Importantp-value



The p-value is the probability, assuming \(H_0\) is true, of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one we observed, in the direction(s) of \(H_1\).
A small p-value means our sample would be unusual if \(H_0\) were true.
Decision rule: reject \(H_0\) if p-value \(< \alpha\); accept \(H_0\) if p-value \(\ge \alpha\).


The p-value is an area beyond the test statistic, in the direction of \(H_1\):



\(H_1\)
p-value




\(<\)
area to the left of the test statistic


\(>\)
area to the right of the test statistic


\(\ne\)
twice the area beyond the test statistic in one tail














(a) H1: <











(b) H1: >











(c) H1: ≠







Figure 3.1: The p-value as an area under the z curve (orange)



The critical-region method and the p-value method always give the same decision: \(z_{\text{cal}}\) falls in the critical region exactly when the p-value is less than \(\alpha\).






WarningWhat the p-value is not



The p-value is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true. It is calculated assuming \(H_0\) is true.




Finding a p-value from the \(z\) Table
Table 4 gives the area to the left of a positive \(z\). To find a p-value:

Round \(|z_{\text{cal}}|\) to 2 decimals and read the area to its left, \(P(Z \le |z_{\text{cal}}|)\).
The area in one tail beyond it is \(1 - P(Z \le |z_{\text{cal}}|)\).
Take one tail for a one-sided test (in the direction of \(H_1\)), or twice that area for a two-sided test.

The p-value is rounded to 4 decimals.


Example
Example 3.2.1. In Example 3.1.1 (household debt, urban vs rural) we tested \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) against \(H_1: p_1 \ne p_2\) and found \(z_{\text{cal}} = -2.153\). Find the p-value and make the decision at \(\alpha\) = 0.05. Compare with the critical-region method.






TipSolution





The test is two-sided, so the p-value is the area in both tails beyond \(\pm2.153\).








Figure 3.2: p-value for Example 3.2.1: the two tails beyond ±2.153





From Table 4, \(P(Z \le 2.15) = 0.9842\), so one tail is \(1 - 0.9842 = 0.0158\) and \[
\text{p-value} = 2(0.0158) = 0.0316.
\]
The test in five steps, with the p-value in Step 4:
Step 1: Hypotheses. \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) \(\quad H_1: p_1 \ne p_2\)
Step 2: Level of significance. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3: Test statistic. \(z_{\text{cal}} = -2.153\) (from Example 3.1.1)
Step 4: p-value. p-value = 0.0316
Step 5: Decision and interpretation. p-value = 0.0316 < \(\alpha\) = 0.05, so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the proportion of households with debt is different in urban and rural areas at the 0.05 level of significance.

Both methods give the same decision.





Your Turn






NoteYour Turn 3.2.1



Find the p-value from Table 4 and make the decision at \(\alpha\) = 0.05.

Your Turn 3.1.1 (brand switching): \(H_1: p_A > p_B\), \(z_{\text{cal}} = 2.032\).
Example 2.1.1 (construction wages): \(H_1: \mu < 380\), \(z_{\text{cal}} = -2.160\).



















TipSolution: Your Turn 3.2.1






Right-sided: p-value = area to the right of \(2.032\). \(P(Z \le 2.03) = 0.9788\), so p-value \(= 1 - 0.9788 = 0.0212\). p-value = 0.0212 < \(\alpha\) = 0.05, so we reject \(H_0\) (the same decision as in Your Turn 3.1.1).
Left-sided: p-value = area to the left of \(-2.160\). By symmetry it equals the area to the right of 2.16: \(1 - 0.9846 = 0.0154\). p-value = 0.0154 < \(\alpha\) = 0.05, so we reject \(H_0\) (the same decision as in Example 2.1.1).






Formula Summary







p-value
probability, assuming \(H_0\) is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed, in the direction of \(H_1\)


From Table 4
one tail \(= 1 - P(Z \le |z_{\text{cal}}|)\); one-sided: p-value = one tail (in the direction of \(H_1\)); two-sided: p-value = 2 × one tail


Decision
reject \(H_0\) if p-value \(< \alpha\); accept \(H_0\) if p-value \(\ge \alpha\)





Exercises
3.2.1 Find the p-value from Table 4 and make the decision at \(\alpha\) = 0.05.

Example 2.3.1 (co-payment scheme): \(H_1: p > 0.30\), \(z_{\text{cal}} = 3.057\).
Exercise 3.1.2 (price displays): \(H_1: p_1 < p_2\), \(z_{\text{cal}} = -1.131\).







TipSolution: Exercise 3.2.1






Right-sided: p-value \(= 1 - P(Z \le 3.06) = 1 - 0.9989 = 0.0011\) < 0.05: reject \(H_0\).
Left-sided: p-value \(= P(Z \le -1.131) = 1 - P(Z \le 1.13) = 1 - 0.8708 = 0.1292\) \(\ge\) 0.05: accept \(H_0\).

Both agree with the critical-region decisions in Sections 2.3 and 3.1.



3.2.2 For each p-value, write the decision at \(\alpha\) = 0.05: (a) 0.0312, (b) 0.0500, (c) 0.1847, (d) 0.0005.






TipSolution: Exercise 3.2.2






0.0312 < 0.05: reject \(H_0\).
0.0500 \(\ge\) 0.05: accept \(H_0\).
0.1847 \(\ge\) 0.05: accept \(H_0\).
0.0005 < 0.05: reject \(H_0\).




3.2.3 A student says: “The p-value is 0.03, so there is a 3% chance that \(H_0\) is true.” Explain what is wrong.






TipSolution: Exercise 3.2.3





The p-value is calculated assuming \(H_0\) is true. It is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the sample result if \(H_0\) were true, not the probability that \(H_0\) is true.

3.3 Reading R Output

Learning Objectives

Read the output of t.test() in R: test statistic, df, p-value, CI and estimate.
Check that R output agrees with a calculation by hand.
Choose the R output whose alternative hypothesis matches the research question.



Concept
In Section 3.2 we found p-values for \(z\) tests from Table 4. For \(t\), \(\chi^2\) and \(F\) the printed tables give only a few areas, so we cannot read an exact p-value from them. Statistical software calculates the p-value for us. The p-value means the same thing as before: an area beyond the test statistic, in the direction of \(H_1\), now under the \(t\) curve.
Example. In Example 2.2.2 (rider earnings, \(H_1: \mu > 600\)), \(t_{\text{cal}} = 2.326\) with df = 24. The p-value is the area to the right of 2.326 under the \(t\) curve, because \(H_1\) points to the right. It is about 0.0144.

title: 3  Two-Sample Inference
text:
3.4 Paired Means

Learning Objectives

Recognize paired data from the way the data were collected.
Reduce paired data to differences \(d\) and use the one-sample \(t\) method on them.
Construct a CI and carry out a test for the mean difference \(\mu_d\), by hand and from R.



Concept
Data are paired when each observation in one group is matched with one observation in the other group. Common designs:

Before and after: the same households are measured before and after a policy.
Matched units: the same products are priced at two shops; twin regions are compared.

Each pair gives one difference \(d = x_1 - x_2\) (for example, after \(-\) before). The pairing removes the variation between units (rich and poor households differ a lot, but each is compared with itself), so we analyse the differences only. A paired test is a one-sample \(t\) test on \(d\) (Section 2.2) with \(H_0: \mu_d = 0\).






ImportantPaired or independent?



Decide from how the data were collected, not from the numbers:

the same units measured twice, or units matched one-to-one → paired
two separate random samples, with no link between a unit in one group and a unit in the other → independent (Section 3.6)

Paired samples always have the same size. Equal sample sizes alone do not make the data paired.




Formulas and Conditions
Conditions: pairs are a random sample; the differences are approximately normal.
With \(n\) pairs, \(\bar{d}\) the mean and \(s_d\) the standard deviation of the differences:
\((1-\alpha)100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu_d\) \[
\bar{d} \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
Test statistic for \(H_0: \mu_d = 0\), with df \(= n-1\) \[
t_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d/\sqrt{n}}
\]
In R: t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE, alternative = ...) uses \(d\) = after \(-\) before (first argument minus second).

title: 3  Two-Sample Inference
text:
3.5 Two Variances

Learning Objectives

Read the \(F\) table (Table 7), including lower-tail values from the reciprocal rule.
Construct and interpret a confidence interval for the ratio \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\).
Test whether two population variances are equal, by hand and with var.test() in R.



Concept
Is one investment riskier than another? Are prices more stable in one market than in another? These questions compare two variances. We compare them with a ratio, not a difference: \[
F = \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}.
\] If the two populations are normal with equal variances, this ratio follows an \(F\) distribution with two degrees of freedom: \(\text{df}_1 = n_1 - 1\) (numerator) and \(\text{df}_2 = n_2 - 1\) (denominator). Like \(\chi^2\), the \(F\) distribution is positive and skewed to the right.
The \(F\) test is also the starting point for the next two topics: Section 3.6 uses it to choose between two \(t\) tests, and Chapter 4 (ANOVA) is built on an \(F\) ratio.


Reading the \(F\) Table
Table 7 gives \(F\) values with area 0.90, 0.95, 0.975, 0.99 or 0.995 to the left, one page for each area. Columns are \(\text{df}_1\) (numerator) and rows are \(\text{df}_2\) (denominator). The order of the df matters.
Areas such as 0.025 and 0.05 are not printed. Use the reciprocal rule, which swaps the two df: \[
F_{\alpha,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2} = \frac{1}{F_{1-\alpha,\,\text{df}_2,\,\text{df}_1}}
\]
Example 3.5.1. Find (a) \(F_{0.95,\,4,\,10}\), (b) \(F_{0.975,\,12,\,15}\), (c) \(F_{0.025,\,12,\,15}\).






TipSolution






Page for 0.95, column 4, row 10: \(F_{0.95,\,4,\,10} = 3.48\).
Page for 0.975, column 12, row 15: \(F_{0.975,\,12,\,15} = 2.96\).
Swap the df and use the 0.975 page: \(F_{0.025,\,12,\,15} = \dfrac{1}{F_{0.975,\,15,\,12}} = \dfrac{1}{3.18} = 0.3145\).









Figure 3.4: Areas 0.025 in each tail of the F distribution with df = (12, 15)














NoteYour Turn 3.5.1



Find (a) \(F_{0.95,\,3,\,20}\), (b) \(F_{0.975,\,8,\,10}\), (c) \(F_{0.025,\,8,\,10}\).





















TipSolution: Your Turn 3.5.1






\(F_{0.95,\,3,\,20} = 3.1\)
\(F_{0.975,\,8,\,10} = 3.85\)
\(F_{0.025,\,8,\,10} = 1/F_{0.975,\,10,\,8} = 1/4.3 = 0.2326\)






Formulas and Conditions
Conditions: two independent random samples from normal populations.
\((1-\alpha)100\%\) confidence interval for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\) \[
\left(\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{1-\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}},\;
      \frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}}\right)
= \left(\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{1-\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}},\;
      \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}\,F_{1-\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_2,\,\text{df}_1}\right)
\] If the interval contains 1, the data are consistent with equal variances.
Test statistic for \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\), with df \(= (n_1-1,\ n_2-1)\) \[
F_{\text{cal}} = \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}
\]







\(H_1\)
Critical region




\(\sigma_1^2 \ne \sigma_2^2\)
\(F_{\text{cal}} < F_{\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}\) or \(F_{\text{cal}} > F_{1-\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}\)


\(\sigma_1^2 < \sigma_2^2\)
\(F_{\text{cal}} < F_{\alpha,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}\)


\(\sigma_1^2 > \sigma_2^2\)
\(F_{\text{cal}} > F_{1-\alpha,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}\)



In R: var.test(x1, x2, alternative = ...) uses \(F = s_1^2/s_2^2\) with x1 in the numerator.


Example
Example 3.5.2. An investor compares the risk of two mutual funds using their monthly returns (%): 13 months for Fund A and 16 months for Fund B. The sample variances are \(s_A^2\) = 6.3586 and \(s_B^2\) = 1.2101. Assume returns are normally distributed.

Construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\sigma_A^2/\sigma_B^2\).
At \(\alpha\) = 0.05, test whether the two funds have different variances (risk).







TipSolution





\(\text{df}_1 = 13 - 1 = 12\), \(\text{df}_2 = 16 - 1 = 15\), \(s_A^2/s_B^2 = 6.3586/1.2101 = 5.255\).
(a) \(F_{0.975,\,12,\,15} = 2.96\) and \(F_{0.975,\,15,\,12} = 3.18\): \[
\left(\frac{5.255}{2.96},\; 5.255 \times 3.18\right)
= (1.7753,\; 16.7109)
\] We are 95% confident that the ratio \(\sigma_A^2/\sigma_B^2\) is between 1.7753 and 16.7109. The interval does not contain 1.
(b)
Step 1: Hypotheses. \(H_0: \sigma_A^2 = \sigma_B^2\) \(\quad H_1: \sigma_A^2 \ne \sigma_B^2\)
Step 2: Level of significance. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3: Test statistic. \[
F_{\text{cal}} = \frac{s_A^2}{s_B^2} = \frac{6.3586}{1.2101} = 5.255,
\qquad \text{df} = (12,\ 15)
\]
Step 4: p-value. From the R output below, p-value = 0.0034. (With the table: critical region \(F_{\text{cal}} < 0.3145\) or \(F_{\text{cal}} > 2.96\).)
Step 5: Decision and interpretation. p-value = 0.0034 < \(\alpha\) = 0.05, so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the variances of the monthly returns of the two funds are different at the 0.05 level of significance; since \(s_A^2 > s_B^2\), Fund A is riskier.

title: 3  Two-Sample Inference
text:
3.6 Two Independent Means

Learning Objectives

Tell independent samples from paired samples by how the data were collected.
Use the \(F\) test to choose between the pooled \(t\) test and the Welch \(t\) test.
Carry out the pooled \(t\) test and CI by hand, and read both tests from R.



Concept
Two independent random samples are drawn from two populations, for example stores using two pricing strategies, or graduates of two universities. We estimate \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) by \(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2\). Its standard error depends on whether the two population variances are equal:

Equal variances (\(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\)): combine the two sample variances into one pooled variance \(s_p^2\) and use the pooled \(t\) test with df \(= n_1 + n_2 - 2\). This is calculated by hand.
Unequal variances: use the Welch \(t\) test. Its df is not a whole number, so we read it from R.

So the method has a first step: compare the variances with the \(F\) test of Section 3.5.






ImportantChoosing the method




Paired or independent? (Section 3.4) If paired, use the paired \(t\) test.
If independent, test \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\) (two-sided, \(\alpha\) = 0.05).

accept \(H_0\) → pooled \(t\) test: t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = TRUE)
reject \(H_0\) → Welch \(t\) test: t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = FALSE)






Formulas and Conditions
Conditions: two independent random samples; both populations approximately normal.
Pooled method (equal variances), df \(= n_1 + n_2 - 2\) \[
s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2},
\qquad
\text{SE} = \sqrt{s_p^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}
\] \[
\text{CI: } (\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n_1+n_2-2}\,\text{SE}
\qquad
t_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\text{SE}}
\]
Welch method (unequal variances): read \(t_{\text{cal}}\), df, p-value and CI from t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = FALSE).







\(H_1\)
Critical region (pooled)




\(\mu_1 \ne \mu_2\)
\(t_{\text{cal}} < t_{\alpha/2,\,\text{df}}\) or \(t_{\text{cal}} > t_{1-\alpha/2,\,\text{df}}\)


\(\mu_1 < \mu_2\)

title: 4  Analysis of Variance
text:
Learning Objectives

Explain why we use ANOVA, not many \(t\) tests, to compare three or more means.
Describe a completely randomized design (CRD) and the assumptions of one-way ANOVA.
Calculate the ANOVA table by hand for a small data set.
Read the output of summary(aov(y ~ trt)) in R and write the conclusion.



Concept
A retail chain wants to compare three pricing strategies. Testing each pair with a \(t\) test needs three tests; with five strategies it needs ten. Each test has a 5% chance of a Type I error, so the chance of at least one false “significant” result grows quickly. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) tests all the means at once: \[
H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \cdots = \mu_k \qquad
H_1: \text{at least one } \mu_i \text{ is different}
\]
In a completely randomized design (CRD) the treatments (here, pricing strategies) are assigned to experimental units (stores) completely at random.
The idea of ANOVA is to split the total variation in the data into two parts:

variation between the treatment means (treatment sum of squares, SSTr)
variation within the treatments (error sum of squares, SSE)

If the treatment means are really equal, the between-treatment variation is only random noise, about the same size as the within-treatment variation. The ratio of the two mean squares is an \(F\) statistic, as in Section 3.5.








Figure 4.1: Weekly sales (hundred units) of 15 stores under three pricing strategies; lines show treatment means

4.2 Multiple Comparisons (Tukey)

Learning Objectives

Explain when a multiple-comparison procedure is needed.
Read the output of TukeyHSD(): difference, confidence interval and adjusted p-value.
Decide which pairs of means differ and write the conclusion.



Concept
When ANOVA rejects \(H_0\), we know that at least one mean is different, but not which ones. Comparing every pair with separate \(t\) tests would raise the overall chance of a Type I error, as Section 4.1 explained.
Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD) method compares every pair of means while keeping the family-wise error rate (the chance of at least one Type I error among all the comparisons) at \(\alpha\) = 0.05. It is based on the Studentized range distribution (Table 14). In this course we read Tukey’s results from R only.






ImportantWhen to use Tukey



Use Tukey only after the ANOVA \(F\) test rejects \(H_0\). If ANOVA accepts \(H_0\), the conclusion is that all the means are equal, and no pairwise comparison is needed.




Reading R Output
TukeyHSD(model) prints one row for each pair of treatments:

Meaning

difference between the two sample means, in the order of the row name (e.g. Discount-Regular = \(\bar{x}_D - \bar{x}_R\))

lower and upper limits of a 95% (family-wise) CI for the difference


p adj
adjusted p-value for \(H_0: \mu_i = \mu_j\)



A pair is significantly different if p adj \(< 0.05\); equivalently, if the CI from lwr to upr does not contain 0.

title: 4  Analysis of Variance
text:
4.3 Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD)

Learning Objectives

Explain what a block is and why blocking makes a comparison more precise.
Describe a randomized complete block design (RCBD).
Calculate the RCBD ANOVA table and read summary(aov(y ~ trt + block)).
Follow a significant result with TukeyHSD(model, "trt").



Concept
Suppose the retail chain from Section 4.1 has stores in five provinces. Sales in Chiang Mai are much higher than in Nan, whatever the pricing strategy. In a CRD this province-to-province variation ends up in the error term, makes MSE large and hides the differences between strategies.
A block is a group of similar experimental units. In a randomized complete block design (RCBD):

every treatment appears once in every block (the design is “complete”);
within each block, the treatments are assigned to units at random.

Here each province is a block: in each province, three stores are randomly assigned to the three strategies. Comparing strategies within each province removes the province effect, and ANOVA separates the variation into three parts: treatments, blocks and error.








Figure 4.2: Weekly sales by strategy in each province. Provinces differ a lot, but within every province the Discount strategy sells most.







Formulas and Conditions
Assumptions: within each block the treatments are assigned at random; the errors are independent and normal with constant variance; no interaction between treatments and blocks.

Which Method? Practice
For each study, name the parameter(s), the method and the section.

The Bank of Thailand wants to know whether the share of households with credit-card debt has risen above 35%.
A researcher compares the mean wage of 40 workers in Chiang Mai with the mean wage of 35 workers in Khon Kaen.
The same 25 firms report their profits before and after a tax change.
An analyst asks whether the daily returns of a stock index have become more volatile than a standard deviation of 1.2%.
Four fertilizer subsidy schemes are each tried in five districts, with the scheme randomly assigned to villages within each district.
A survey compares the proportion of men and of women who own a business.







TipSolution: Which Method? Practice






One proportion, \(z\) test for \(p\) (2.3), \(H_1: p > 0.35\).
Two independent means: \(F\) test for the variances first, then pooled or Welch \(t\) (3.5, 3.6).
Paired means: paired \(t\) test on the differences (3.4).
One variance: chi-square test, \(H_1: \sigma^2 > 1.44\) (2.4).
Four means with blocks (districts): RCBD ANOVA (4.3), then Tukey if \(H_0\) is rejected.
Two proportions: \(z\) test for \(p_1 - p_2\) (3.1).

text:
Mixed Problems
Use \(\alpha\) = 0.05 and the five steps.

M1
In a survey of 500 workers, 210 have a second job. Test whether more than 40% of workers have a second job. Use the critical region.






TipSolution: M1





One proportion (2.3). \(\hat{p} = 210/500 = 0.42\).
Step 1. \(H_0: p = 0.40 \quad H_1: p > 0.40\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3. \(\sqrt{0.40(0.60)/500} = 0.0219\); \(z_{\text{cal}} = (0.42 - 0.40)/0.0219 = 0.913\)
Step 4. Critical region: \(z_{\text{cal}} > 1.645\).
Step 5. \(z_{\text{cal}} = 0.913\) does not fall in the critical region (\(0.913 < 1.645\)), so we accept \(H_0\). That is, the proportion of workers with a second job is equal to 0.40 at the 0.05 level of significance.





M2
The monthly profit (thousand baht) of 9 cafés in the old city has \(\bar{x}\) = 52.4, \(s\) = 6.1; that of 13 cafés near the university has \(\bar{x}\) = 47.8, \(s\) = 5.4. (a) Use the \(F\) test with the critical region to check the variances. (b) Test whether the mean profits are different, using the critical region.






TipSolution: M2





(a) \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\) vs \(H_1: \sigma_1^2 \ne \sigma_2^2\). \(F_{\text{cal}} = 37.21/29.16 = 1.276\), df = (8, 12). Critical region: \(F_{\text{cal}} < 1/F_{0.975,\,12,\,8} = 0.2381\) or \(F_{\text{cal}} > F_{0.975,\,8,\,12} = 3.51\). \(F_{\text{cal}}\) does not fall in the critical region, so we accept \(H_0\): the variances are equal. Use the pooled \(t\) test.
(b)
Step 1. \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 \quad H_1: \mu_1 \ne \mu_2\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3. \(s_p^2 = [8(37.21) + 12(29.16)]/20 = 32.38\); SE \(= \sqrt{32.38(1/9 + 1/13)} = 2.4675\); \(t_{\text{cal}} = (52.4 - 47.8)/2.4675 = 1.864\), df = 20
Step 4. Critical region: \(t_{\text{cal}} < -2.086\) or \(t_{\text{cal}} > 2.086\).
Step 5. \(t_{\text{cal}} = 1.864\) does not fall in the critical region (\(-2.086 < 1.864 < 2.086\)), so we accept \(H_0\). That is, the mean monthly profits of cafés in the two areas are equal at the 0.05 level of significance.





M3
A central bank wants the standard deviation of the monthly inflation rate to be less than 1 percentage point. Over 15 months, \(s\) = 0.8. Assume normality and test whether the target is met, using the critical region.






TipSolution: M3





One variance (2.4).
Step 1. \(H_0: \sigma^2 = 1 \quad H_1: \sigma^2 < 1\)
Step 2. \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Step 3. \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = 14(0.64)/1 = 8.960\), df = 14
Step 4. \(\chi^2_{0.05,\,14} = 6.57\). Critical region: \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} < 6.57\).
Step 5. \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} = 8.960\) does not fall in the critical region (\(8.960 > 6.57\)), so we accept \(H_0\). That is, the standard deviation of monthly inflation is equal to 1 percentage point at the 0.05 level of significance; the data do not show that the target is met.

title: Summary: Choosing a Method
text:
Writing a Full Conclusion
A full conclusion has a decision and an interpretation in the words of the problem:

Decision. [statistic or p-value] … so we [reject / accept] \(H_0\). Interpretation. That is, … at the 0.05 level of significance.

Checklist:

If you reject \(H_0\), write \(H_1\) as a sentence; if you accept \(H_0\), write \(H_0\) as a sentence.
Name the population and the variable (not just “the mean”).
For a two-sided test that rejects \(H_0\), add the direction from the sample statistics.
For ANOVA, “not all equal”; then use Tukey to say which ones differ.

Write the decision and the interpretation for each result.

\(H_0: \mu = 15000\), \(H_1: \mu \ne 15000\) for the mean monthly rent (baht) in a district; \(t_{\text{cal}} = -2.514\), critical region \(|t_{\text{cal}}| > 2.064\), \(\bar{x}\) = 13,850.
\(H_0: p_1 = p_2\), \(H_1: p_1 > p_2\) for the proportions of urban (1) and rural (2) households using mobile banking; p-value = 0.0832.
One-way ANOVA comparing mean loan sizes at three types of lender; p-value = 0.0007.







TipSolution: Writing a Full Conclusion






\(t_{\text{cal}} = -2.514\) falls in the critical region (\(-2.514 < -2.064\)), so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the mean monthly rent in the district is different from 15,000 baht at the 0.05 level of significance; since \(\bar{x}\) = 13,850, it is lower than 15,000 baht.
p-value = 0.0832 \(\ge\) \(\alpha\) = 0.05, so we accept \(H_0\). That is, the proportions of urban and rural households using mobile banking are equal at the 0.05 level of significance.
p-value = 0.0007 < \(\alpha\) = 0.05, so we reject \(H_0\). That is, the mean loan sizes are not all equal across the three types of lender at the 0.05 level of significance. (Use Tukey’s method to find which types differ.)
